segments.title: Hiroshima as a thriving city beside its memorials
segments.summary: A view from the memorial area leads to a reflection on Hiroshima as a living, rebuilt city rather than a place frozen by the bombing.
segments.body: The visit overturns an expectation that Hiroshima would be defined by the atomic bombing. It finds a busy and attractive modern city built around the places that preserve its past. From the memorial area near the dome, the view extends across ground described as having been scooped out by the blast and toward the rebuilt city beyond it. Commemoration and recovery occupy the same urban landscape. The personal recommendation to visit the memorial and museum sets up the more intimate reflection that follows.

evidence.note: He contrasts an expectation of a city defined by its past with the thriving city seen from the memorial area and calls the museum devastatingly effective.

segments.title: Museum objects and the human cost of the Hiroshima bombing
segments.summary: The Hiroshima museum makes familiar facts about the bombing immediate through stories of illness, bereavement, and a school uniform made from pieces belonging to three children who died.
segments.body: Familiar facts and figures about the bombing feel different when encountered through the museum's objects and personal stories. One account concerns a girl who developed cancer after the bomb and still tried to keep others happy. A small school uniform assembled from surviving pieces belonging to three children who died has even greater emotional force. Its resemblance to a remembered primary-school uniform makes the victims imaginable as ordinary school friends. The passage is a personal response rather than a detailed history of the bombing. The museum objects make civilian suffering immediate.

evidence.note: He contrasts facts and figures with museum stories of cancer after the bomb and a school uniform made from three dead children's remains.
